intro: The solar system, the night sky and space exploration, plus the horoscope that everyone reads and nobody believes.
b1.texto:
**What is up there.** **El universo** contains **galaxias**; ours is **la Vía Láctea**. **El sistema solar** has eight **planetas**: Mercurio, Venus, **la Tierra**, Marte, Júpiter, Saturno, Urano and Neptuno. Note the capital: **la Tierra** is the planet, **la tierra** is soil or land.

**Movement.** La Tierra **gira alrededor del** Sol y **sobre sí misma**. La Luna **está en órbita**. Las estrellas **brillan**.

**The Sun.** **El sol sale** and **se pone**. The moments: **el amanecer** and **el atardecer**; **al amanecer**, **al anochecer**. These are infinitives used as nouns, and also verbs: **amanece** a las siete.

**The Moon.** **Luna llena**, **luna nueva**, **cuarto creciente**, **cuarto menguante**. **Un eclipse de sol** or **de luna**, **total** or **parcial**.

**The night sky.** **Una constelación**, like **la Osa Mayor**. **Una estrella fugaz** (a shooting star). **Un cometa**. Distances are measured in **años luz**.

**Exploration.** **Un astrónomo** uses **un telescopio**. **Un astronauta** travels in **una nave espacial** after **el lanzamiento** of **un cohete**. **Una estación espacial.** **Un satélite.** **La gravedad.**

**Astrology.** Not the same as **la astronomía**. **¿De qué signo eres? Soy** leo. The signs take no capital when they describe a person: **es** capricornio.

**Idioms.** **Estar en la luna** (to be miles away). **Pedir la luna** (to ask for the impossible). **Ver las estrellas** (to see stars, with pain). **Nacer con estrella** (to be born lucky).
b2.f0: On 12 August 2026, for the first time in more than a century, a total eclipse of the sun could be seen from the Iberian Peninsula.
b2.f1: Such an eclipse happens when the Moon places itself exactly between the Earth and the Sun and covers it completely.
b2.f2: It is an extraordinary coincidence: the Sun is four hundred times bigger than the Moon, but it is four hundred times further away.
b2.f3: For a little over a minute night fell shortly before sunset, the temperature dropped and some stars shone.
b2.f4: The birds stopped singing, as if night had really come.
b2.f5: Astronomers had insisted that nobody should look at the Sun without special glasses, however brief the moment might be.
b2.f6: Those who saw it say they understood why, for thousands of years, eclipses were so frightening.
b4.pregunta: According to the text, why can the Moon cover the Sun exactly?
b4.o1.refuerzo: It is four hundred times smaller.
b4.o2.refuerzo: The text does not say that.
b5.pregunta: According to the text, what did the birds do?
b5.o0.refuerzo: Dejaron de cantar, como si hubiera llegado la noche.
b5.o1.refuerzo: The text does not say that.
b6.pregunta: Complete: the Earth revolves around the Sun.
b6.o2.refuerzo: Ponerse is to set, said of the Sun.
b7.pregunta: Siempre estás en la luna means…
b7.o0.refuerzo: Estar en la luna: to be distracted.
b8.o0.refuerzo: Por + adjective + que takes the subjunctive.
b9.o1: The sun gets dressed at nine.
b9.o1.explicacion: Ponerse, of the sun: to set.
b10.traduccion: At dawn a few stars were still shining.

**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (150–180 words).** Write the account of a natural phenomenon you have seen: an eclipse, a storm, a starry sky.

**Speak (about 3 minutes).** Debate aloud: is space exploration worth the money?
